opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling is still the foundation, but the question has shifted from "who can scale the most" to "who can scale the right things efficiently."

In the early phase, the advantage seemed to belong to whoever had the most compute and data. Bigger models, more tokens, and the results kept improving. That logic hasn't disappeared; compute still matters a lot. But many teams have now seen that simply piling on resources has diminishing returns if your architecture, data, and training recipes aren't well designed. So the leading teams will be the ones that make smart scaling decisions: where to put the next unit of compute, whether into pretraining, post-training, reinforcement learning, or inference-time reasoning.

Efficiency has become a competitive weapon. If you can reach similar capability at a fraction of the cost through better model structure, better data, or better infrastructure, you can iterate faster, run more experiments, and serve more users. Over time, that iteration speed compounds. A team that runs ten good experiments while another runs one expensive one will often learn more.

I also think reinforcement learning and reasoning have opened a new scaling dimension. We're still early in understanding its scaling laws. Teams that identify what actually scales there, and which signals and environments give real improvement rather than benchmark overfitting, will have a big edge.

So in the next phase, the leaders won't be decided by resources alone. Resources are the entry ticket. What separates teams is research taste, engineering discipline, and the courage to bet on directions before everyone agrees they're right. Talent density and organizational focus matter as much as GPU count.

r001.rationale: It contrasts simply scaling more with scaling the right things efficiently, naming compute allocation across pretraining, post-training, reinforcement learning, and inference-time reasoning as alternative targets.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling choices shaping future leadership, but gives no time horizon such as six months or more.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think scaling decisions are really the hidden fork in the road for every team right now, because they're not just technical choices, they're bets about what kind of organization you want to be.

The first thing I'd say is that scaling has stopped being a single knob. For a long time the story was simple: more parameters, more data, more compute, and the loss curve rewards you. That's still true in a narrow sense, but the marginal return on just making the base model bigger has become much more expensive to capture. So the interesting decisions now are about where you spend. Do you put compute into pretraining, into post-training and reinforcement learning, into inference-time reasoning, or into data quality and synthetic data pipelines? Teams that treat those as one budget and allocate deliberately are pulling ahead of teams that just chase the biggest dense model.

The second thing is efficiency as a strategic lever rather than an afterthought. When I think about why some groups have been able to compete without the largest clusters, it comes down to architectural and systems choices: mixture-of-experts, better attention and memory handling, training stability at scale, very careful engineering of the whole stack. Those choices let you turn a fixed amount of compute into much more effective capability. In an environment where access to hardware is uneven, the teams that are forced to be efficient sometimes end up with a durable advantage, because they build the muscle early.

Third, I think leadership increasingly belongs to whoever closes the loop between the model and real use. Scaling pretraining gives you raw capability; but the signals that tell you what to scale next come from reasoning benchmarks, from agents actually doing tasks, from users. The groups that can run that cycle fast, train, deploy, observe, adjust the recipe, are learning faster than those that run one giant training run a year and hope.

And finally, the human side. A lot of these decisions are made by small groups of researchers who have the judgment to say, this direction is worth ten thousand GPUs and that one isn't. That judgment is scarce. So I'd say the next phase will be led less by whoever has the most compute in absolute terms, and more by whoever combines serious compute with the taste and the engineering discipline to spend it well. Open models have shown that quite clearly: good decisions compound, and they can narrow gaps that looked permanent.

r001.rationale: It contrasts growing the base model’s parameter count with allocating compute to post-training, inference-time reasoning, and data quality.

r002.rationale: It says scaling choices shape who leads the next phase, but gives no timeframe of roughly six months or more.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what you choose to scale. More compute, more data, and larger models can improve capability, but the decision is also about where you expect the next bottleneck to be. If you keep investing in one direction after its returns start to diminish, scale becomes a very expensive commitment.

So I would look at how well a team learns from smaller experiments before making those commitments. Can they distinguish a limitation in the architecture from a problem with data quality or training? Can they turn that understanding into a better use of their next unit of compute?

Resources will matter, of course. But I don’t think leadership is settled simply by who can afford the largest training run. It will also depend on who makes the right scaling decisions—and who recognizes quickly when those decisions need to change.

r001.rationale: The response asks what to scale and contrasts compute and data with larger models, raising whether scaling should focus on model size or another quantity.

r002.rationale: The response connects scaling decisions to who leads, but gives no timeframe of roughly six months or more.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling decisions reveal what a team believes is actually limiting progress. Is it compute, data quality, the training method, or the model’s ability to learn from feedback? If you identify the wrong bottleneck, you can spend much more and gain very little.

So leadership won’t simply belong to whoever trains the largest model. It will depend on who can run informative experiments, turn those results into better architecture and training decisions, and then scale what works. Efficiency matters because it lets you test more ideas with the same resources.

There’s also a balance between training and inference. A stronger model is valuable, but the cost of using it determines how widely people can benefit from it. I would look for teams that improve capability and make that capability affordable. Those two things together will shape who leads the next phase.

r001.rationale: It contrasts leadership through training the largest model with identifying other bottlenecks and scaling what works, raising model size versus other scaling targets.
